case_info.scenario: A previously healthy individual in his 20s presented to the dermatology clinic for evaluation of annular skin lesions that appeared first on his right ankle and then on other areas of his body over a 3-month period. He reported numbness and paresthesia in the areas of affected skin and an inability to fully extend his fingers. The patient did not take any prescription medications or herbal supplements and had immigrated to the US from Samoa 4 years prior. Physical examination revealed multiple tattoos and annular erythematous plaques on his face, chest (Figure, left panel), back, arms, and legs. The patient had bilateral palpable thickened auricular and ulnar nerves, claw-hand deformity (Figure, right panel), foot drop bilaterally, and decreased sensation to temperature over the areas of skin plaque. Results of testing for rapid plasma reagin, antinuclear antibodies, and rheumatoid factor were negative. Examination of punch biopsy samples from 2 plaques on his back revealed granulomatous periadnexal and perivascular dermatitis with diffuse granulomatous infiltrate and foamy histiocytes. Findings on acid-fast bacilli stains and mycobacterial polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing were negative. Repeat biopsy of a skin plaque revealed no fungal organisms, andMycobacterium lepraewas not identified on Fite Faraco stain.

case_info.explanation: C. Send skin biopsy specimen to the US National Hansen’s Disease Program for PCR testing The key to the correct diagnosis was the presence of skin lesions with associated hypoesthesia and peripheral nerve abnormalities in a patient from Samoa, where leprosy is endemic. Choice A is incorrect because the mycobacteria causing leprosy cannot be cultured on chocolate agar.1Serologic testing forM lepraephenolic glycolipid 1 (choice B) is not commonly performed due to low sensitivity.2Choice D is incorrect because the diagnosis of leprosy must be confirmed before starting dapsone, rifampin, and clofazimine. Leprosy, also known as Hansen disease, is an infection caused by the acid-fast bacilliM lepraeandMycobacterium lepromatosis,which are obligate intracellular organisms that cannot be cultured on artificial media.1Humans are the primary carriers of infection, and in the US, the 9-banded armadillo is a zoonotic reservoir.1,3Approximately 200 000 individuals worldwide and 200 to 300 people in the US are diagnosed with leprosy annually.4,5The most common route of transmission is through respiratory secretions, but skin contamination with tattooing and vertical transmission have been reported.1,6Risk factors include close contact with a patient recently diagnosed with leprosy, immunosuppression, immunodeficiency, genetic predisposition, and exposure to armadillos.1The differential diagnosis of leprosy includes interstitial granulomatous dermatitis, granuloma annulare, granulomatous dermatitis of immune deficiency, granulomatous drug eruption, psoriasis, and other mycobacterial or fungal infections.7 The World Health Organization (WHO) classifies leprosy as multibacillary if there are 6 or more skin lesions or as paucibacillary if there fewer than 6 skin lesions.7The Ridley-Jopling classification system defines 5 categories of leprosy: tuberculoid, borderline tuberculoid, borderline, borderline lepromatous, and lepromatous.7 The clinical diagnosis of leprosy is based on the typical signs of skin lesions with hypoesthesia and nerve enlargement.7Some patients may develop an immune response toM leprae, called a leprosy reaction, which presents as urticarial swelling of skin lesions, fever, neuritis, erythema nodosum, and permanent loss of motor and sensory nerve function.2,8Leprosy reactions can occur before, during, or after treatment for leprosy.5,8 Skin biopsy is the only laboratory test that can definitively diagnose leprosy.7If skin biopsy is nondiagnostic, PCR testing of a skin biopsy specimen may be helpful. PCR has a sensitivity of 34% to 80% for paucibacillary leprosy and greater than 90% sensitivity for multibacillary leprosy, with a specificity of up to 100% for both paucibacillary and multibacillary leprosy.9 Early diagnosis and treatment are important to decrease disability and adverse psychosocial effects of leprosy and to reduce the risk of transmission.2,10The WHO recommends a 6-month course of dapsone, rifampin, and clofazimine for paucibacillary leprosy and a 12-month course for multibacillary leprosy.2Treatment with rifampin, moxifloxacin, and minocycline taken monthly for 12 to 24 months has similar efficacy, fewer adverse effects, and improved adherence compared with the WHO regimen but is 4 times more expensive.5 Leprosy relapse rates after completion of WHO multidrug therapy are 0.77% for multibacillary leprosy and 1.07% for paucibacillary leprosy.8Relapse rates appear similar after completing the regimen of rifampin, moxifloxacin, and minocycline.5Risk factors for relapse include high mycobacterial load, increased number of skin lesions, insufficient treatment duration or regimen, and poor treatment adherence.4,8 A skin biopsy sample from the patient’s arm sent to the US National Hansen’s Disease Program tested positive forM lepraeusing a quantitative PCR assay. The patient received prednisone (60 mg daily) for 5 days, then prednisone (5 mg daily) and methotrexate (20 mg weekly) to treat a leprosy reaction, which manifested as worsening paresthesia and erythema in existing skin plaques. Six days later, he started a monthly regimen of rifampin (600 mg), moxifloxacin (400 mg), and minocycline (100 mg) and received amitriptyline (10 mg) for neuropathic pain. Two months after initiation of antibiotics, the skin lesions and neuropathy symptoms had substantially improved. Eleven months after presentation, the patient underwent tendon transfer surgery with a fascia lata graft to the second through fifth fingers on his left hand, after which he completed 3 months of occupational therapy. At his most recent clinic visit, he had taken 9 of 12 planned months of rifampin, moxifloxacin, and minocycline and was taking prednisone (5 mg daily) and methotrexate (20 mg weekly).

dialogue_history.text: I agree that leprosy is the leading diagnosis, but serologic testing for phenolic glycolipid 1 has variable sensitivity and is not typically the definitive confirmatory step. The gold standard is a skin biopsy with specific stains (Fite-Faraco) and PCR for M. leprae, which was negative here. Given the high clinical suspicion, a repeat biopsy from a different site, such as the thickened nerve, for PCR and histopathology would be more reliable.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid

   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

A previously healthy individual in his 20s presented to the dermatology clinic for evaluation of annular skin lesions that appeared first on his right ankle and then on other areas of his body over a 3-month period. He reported numbness and paresthesia in the areas of affected skin and an inability to fully extend his fingers. The patient did not take any prescription medications or herbal supplements and had immigrated to the US from Samoa 4 years prior. Physical examination revealed multiple tattoos and annular erythematous plaques on his face, chest (Figure, left panel), back, arms, and legs. The patient had bilateral palpable thickened auricular and ulnar nerves, claw-hand deformity (Figure, right panel), foot drop bilaterally, and decreased sensation to temperature over the areas of skin plaque. Results of testing for rapid plasma reagin, antinuclear antibodies, and rheumatoid factor were negative. Examination of punch biopsy samples from 2 plaques on his back revealed granulomatous periadnexal and perivascular dermatitis with diffuse granulomatous infiltrate and foamy histiocytes. Findings on acid-fast bacilli stains and mycobacterial polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing were negative. Repeat biopsy of a skin plaque revealed no fungal organisms, andMycobacterium lepraewas not identified on Fite Faraco stain.

case_info.explanation: C. Send skin biopsy specimen to the US National Hansen’s Disease Program for PCR testing The key to the correct diagnosis was the presence of skin lesions with associated hypoesthesia and peripheral nerve abnormalities in a patient from Samoa, where leprosy is endemic. Choice A is incorrect because the mycobacteria causing leprosy cannot be cultured on chocolate agar.1Serologic testing forM lepraephenolic glycolipid 1 (choice B) is not commonly performed due to low sensitivity.2Choice D is incorrect because the diagnosis of leprosy must be confirmed before starting dapsone, rifampin, and clofazimine. Leprosy, also known as Hansen disease, is an infection caused by the acid-fast bacilliM lepraeandMycobacterium lepromatosis,which are obligate intracellular organisms that cannot be cultured on artificial media.1Humans are the primary carriers of infection, and in the US, the 9-banded armadillo is a zoonotic reservoir.1,3Approximately 200 000 individuals worldwide and 200 to 300 people in the US are diagnosed with leprosy annually.4,5The most common route of transmission is through respiratory secretions, but skin contamination with tattooing and vertical transmission have been reported.1,6Risk factors include close contact with a patient recently diagnosed with leprosy, immunosuppression, immunodeficiency, genetic predisposition, and exposure to armadillos.1The differential diagnosis of leprosy includes interstitial granulomatous dermatitis, granuloma annulare, granulomatous dermatitis of immune deficiency, granulomatous drug eruption, psoriasis, and other mycobacterial or fungal infections.7 The World Health Organization (WHO) classifies leprosy as multibacillary if there are 6 or more skin lesions or as paucibacillary if there fewer than 6 skin lesions.7The Ridley-Jopling classification system defines 5 categories of leprosy: tuberculoid, borderline tuberculoid, borderline, borderline lepromatous, and lepromatous.7 The clinical diagnosis of leprosy is based on the typical signs of skin lesions with hypoesthesia and nerve enlargement.7Some patients may develop an immune response toM leprae, called a leprosy reaction, which presents as urticarial swelling of skin lesions, fever, neuritis, erythema nodosum, and permanent loss of motor and sensory nerve function.2,8Leprosy reactions can occur before, during, or after treatment for leprosy.5,8 Skin biopsy is the only laboratory test that can definitively diagnose leprosy.7If skin biopsy is nondiagnostic, PCR testing of a skin biopsy specimen may be helpful. PCR has a sensitivity of 34% to 80% for paucibacillary leprosy and greater than 90% sensitivity for multibacillary leprosy, with a specificity of up to 100% for both paucibacillary and multibacillary leprosy.9 Early diagnosis and treatment are important to decrease disability and adverse psychosocial effects of leprosy and to reduce the risk of transmission.2,10The WHO recommends a 6-month course of dapsone, rifampin, and clofazimine for paucibacillary leprosy and a 12-month course for multibacillary leprosy.2Treatment with rifampin, moxifloxacin, and minocycline taken monthly for 12 to 24 months has similar efficacy, fewer adverse effects, and improved adherence compared with the WHO regimen but is 4 times more expensive.5 Leprosy relapse rates after completion of WHO multidrug therapy are 0.77% for multibacillary leprosy and 1.07% for paucibacillary leprosy.8Relapse rates appear similar after completing the regimen of rifampin, moxifloxacin, and minocycline.5Risk factors for relapse include high mycobacterial load, increased number of skin lesions, insufficient treatment duration or regimen, and poor treatment adherence.4,8 A skin biopsy sample from the patient’s arm sent to the US National Hansen’s Disease Program tested positive forM lepraeusing a quantitative PCR assay. The patient received prednisone (60 mg daily) for 5 days, then prednisone (5 mg daily) and methotrexate (20 mg weekly) to treat a leprosy reaction, which manifested as worsening paresthesia and erythema in existing skin plaques. Six days later, he started a monthly regimen of rifampin (600 mg), moxifloxacin (400 mg), and minocycline (100 mg) and received amitriptyline (10 mg) for neuropathic pain. Two months after initiation of antibiotics, the skin lesions and neuropathy symptoms had substantially improved. Eleven months after presentation, the patient underwent tendon transfer surgery with a fascia lata graft to the second through fifth fingers on his left hand, after which he completed 3 months of occupational therapy. At his most recent clinic visit, he had taken 9 of 12 planned months of rifampin, moxifloxacin, and minocycline and was taking prednisone (5 mg daily) and methotrexate (20 mg weekly).

1. Mental Demand
   Definition:

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.

     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication

   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We

       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the

case_info.explanation: C. Send skin biopsy specimen to the US National Hansen’s Disease Program for PCR testing The key to the correct diagnosis was the presence of skin lesions with associated hypoesthesia and peripheral nerve abnormalities in a patient from Samoa, where leprosy is endemic. Choice A is incorrect because the mycobacteria causing leprosy cannot be cultured on chocolate agar.1Serologic testing forM lepraephenolic glycolipid 1 (choice B) is not commonly performed due to low sensitivity.2Choice D is incorrect because the diagnosis of leprosy must be confirmed before starting dapsone, rifampin, and clofazimine. Leprosy, also known as Hansen disease, is an infection caused by the acid-fast bacilliM lepraeandMycobacterium lepromatosis,which are obligate intracellular organisms that cannot be cultured on artificial media.1Humans are the primary carriers of infection, and in the US, the 9-banded armadillo is a zoonotic reservoir.1,3Approximately 200 000 individuals worldwide and 200 to 300 people in the US are diagnosed with leprosy annually.4,5The most common route of transmission is through respiratory secretions, but skin contamination with tattooing and vertical transmission have been reported.1,6Risk factors include close contact with a patient recently diagnosed with leprosy, immunosuppression, immunodeficiency, genetic predisposition, and exposure to armadillos.1The differential diagnosis of leprosy includes interstitial granulomatous dermatitis, granuloma annulare, granulomatous dermatitis of immune deficiency, granulomatous drug eruption, psoriasis, and other mycobacterial or fungal infections.7 The World Health Organization (WHO) classifies leprosy as multibacillary if there are 6 or more skin lesions or as paucibacillary if there fewer than 6 skin lesions.7The Ridley-Jopling classification system defines 5 categories of leprosy: tuberculoid, borderline tuberculoid, borderline, borderline lepromatous, and lepromatous.7 The clinical diagnosis of leprosy is based on the typical signs of skin lesions with hypoesthesia and nerve enlargement.7Some patients may develop an immune response toM leprae, called a leprosy reaction, which presents as urticarial swelling of skin lesions, fever, neuritis, erythema nodosum, and permanent loss of motor and sensory nerve function.2,8Leprosy reactions can occur before, during, or after treatment for leprosy.5,8 Skin biopsy is the only laboratory test that can definitively diagnose leprosy.7If skin biopsy is nondiagnostic, PCR testing of a skin biopsy specimen may be helpful. PCR has a sensitivity of 34% to 80% for paucibacillary leprosy and greater than 90% sensitivity for multibacillary leprosy, with a specificity of up to 100% for both paucibacillary and multibacillary leprosy.9 Early diagnosis and treatment are important to decrease disability and adverse psychosocial effects of leprosy and to reduce the risk of transmission.2,10The WHO recommends a 6-month course of dapsone, rifampin, and clofazimine for paucibacillary leprosy and a 12-month course for multibacillary leprosy.2Treatment with rifampin, moxifloxacin, and minocycline taken monthly for 12 to 24 months has similar efficacy, fewer adverse effects, and improved adherence compared with the WHO regimen but is 4 times more expensive.5 Leprosy relapse rates after completion of WHO multidrug therapy are 0.77% for multibacillary leprosy and 1.07% for paucibacillary leprosy.8Relapse rates appear similar after completing the regimen of rifampin, moxifloxacin, and minocycline.5Risk factors for relapse include high mycobacterial load, increased number of skin lesions, insufficient treatment duration or regimen, and poor treatment adherence.4,8 A skin biopsy sample from the patient’s arm sent to the US National Hansen’s Disease Program tested positive forM lepraeusing a quantitative PCR assay. The patient received prednisone (60 mg daily) for 5 days, then prednisone (5 mg daily) and methotrexate (20 mg weekly) to treat a leprosy reaction, which manifested as worsening paresthesia and erythema in existing skin plaques. Six days later, he started a monthly regimen of rifampin (600 mg), moxifloxacin (400 mg), and minocycline (100 mg) and received amitriptyline (10 mg) for neuropathic pain. Two months after initiation of antibiotics, the skin lesions and neuropathy symptoms had substantially improved. Eleven months after presentation, the patient underwent tendon transfer surgery with a fascia lata graft to the second through fifth fingers on his left hand, after which he completed 3 months of occupational therapy. At his most recent clinic visit, he had taken 9 of 12 planned months of rifampin, moxifloxacin, and minocycline and was taking prednisone (5 mg daily) and methotrexate (20 mg weekly).

case_info.explanation: C. Send skin biopsy specimen to the US National Hansen’s Disease Program for PCR testing The key to the correct diagnosis was the presence of skin lesions with associated hypoesthesia and peripheral nerve abnormalities in a patient from Samoa, where leprosy is endemic. Choice A is incorrect because the mycobacteria causing leprosy cannot be cultured on chocolate agar.1Serologic testing forM lepraephenolic glycolipid 1 (choice B) is not commonly performed due to low sensitivity.2Choice D is incorrect because the diagnosis of leprosy must be confirmed before starting dapsone, rifampin, and clofazimine. Leprosy, also known as Hansen disease, is an infection caused by the acid-fast bacilliM lepraeandMycobacterium lepromatosis,which are obligate intracellular organisms that cannot be cultured on artificial media.1Humans are the primary carriers of infection, and in the US, the 9-banded armadillo is a zoonotic reservoir.1,3Approximately 200 000 individuals worldwide and 200 to 300 people in the US are diagnosed with leprosy annually.4,5The most common route of transmission is through respiratory secretions, but skin contamination with tattooing and vertical transmission have been reported.1,6Risk factors include close contact with a patient recently diagnosed with leprosy, immunosuppression, immunodeficiency, genetic predisposition, and exposure to armadillos.1The differential diagnosis of leprosy includes interstitial granulomatous dermatitis, granuloma annulare, granulomatous dermatitis of immune deficiency, granulomatous drug eruption, psoriasis, and other mycobacterial or fungal infections.7 The World Health Organization (WHO) classifies leprosy as multibacillary if there are 6 or more skin lesions or as paucibacillary if there fewer than 6 skin lesions.7The Ridley-Jopling classification system defines 5 categories of leprosy: tuberculoid, borderline tuberculoid, borderline, borderline lepromatous, and lepromatous.7 The clinical diagnosis of leprosy is based on the typical signs of skin lesions with hypoesthesia and nerve enlargement.7Some patients may develop an immune response toM leprae, called a leprosy reaction, which presents as urticarial swelling of skin lesions, fever, neuritis, erythema nodosum, and permanent loss of motor and sensory nerve function.2,8Leprosy reactions can occur before, during, or after treatment for leprosy.5,8 Skin biopsy is the only laboratory test that can definitively diagnose leprosy.7If skin biopsy is nondiagnostic, PCR testing of a skin biopsy specimen may be helpful. PCR has a sensitivity of 34% to 80% for paucibacillary leprosy and greater than 90% sensitivity for multibacillary leprosy, with a specificity of up to 100% for both paucibacillary and multibacillary leprosy.9 Early diagnosis and treatment are important to decrease disability and adverse psychosocial effects of leprosy and to reduce the risk of transmission.2,10The WHO recommends a 6-month course of dapsone, rifampin, and clofazimine for paucibacillary leprosy and a 12-month course for multibacillary leprosy.2Treatment with rifampin, moxifloxacin, and minocycline taken monthly for 12 to 24 months has similar efficacy, fewer adverse effects, and improved adherence compared with the WHO regimen but is 4 times more expensive.5 Leprosy relapse rates after completion of WHO multidrug therapy are 0.77% for multibacillary leprosy and 1.07% for paucibacillary leprosy.8Relapse rates appear similar after completing the regimen of rifampin, moxifloxacin, and minocycline.5Risk factors for relapse include high mycobacterial load, increased number of skin lesions, insufficient treatment duration or regimen, and poor treatment adherence.4,8 A skin biopsy sample from the patient’s arm sent to the US National Hansen’s Disease Program tested positive forM lepraeusing a quantitative PCR assay. The patient received prednisone (60 mg daily) for 5 days, then prednisone (5 mg daily) and methotrexate (20 mg weekly) to treat a leprosy reaction, which manifested as worsening paresthesia and erythema in existing skin plaques. Six days later, he started a monthly regimen of rifampin (600 mg), moxifloxacin (400 mg), and minocycline (100 mg) and received amitriptyline (10 mg) for neuropathic pain. Two months after initiation of antibiotics, the skin lesions and neuropathy symptoms had substantially improved. Eleven months after presentation, the patient underwent tendon transfer surgery with a fascia lata graft to the second through fifth fingers on his left hand, after which he completed 3 months of occupational therapy. At his most recent clinic visit, he had taken 9 of 12 planned months of rifampin, moxifloxacin, and minocycline and was taking prednisone (5 mg daily) and methotrexate (20 mg weekly).

case_info.explanation: C. Send skin biopsy specimen to the US National Hansen’s Disease Program for PCR testing The key to the correct diagnosis was the presence of skin lesions with associated hypoesthesia and peripheral nerve abnormalities in a patient from Samoa, where leprosy is endemic. Choice A is incorrect because the mycobacteria causing leprosy cannot be cultured on chocolate agar.1Serologic testing forM lepraephenolic glycolipid 1 (choice B) is not commonly performed due to low sensitivity.2Choice D is incorrect because the diagnosis of leprosy must be confirmed before starting dapsone, rifampin, and clofazimine. Leprosy, also known as Hansen disease, is an infection caused by the acid-fast bacilliM lepraeandMycobacterium lepromatosis,which are obligate intracellular organisms that cannot be cultured on artificial media.1Humans are the primary carriers of infection, and in the US, the 9-banded armadillo is a zoonotic reservoir.1,3Approximately 200 000 individuals worldwide and 200 to 300 people in the US are diagnosed with leprosy annually.4,5The most common route of transmission is through respiratory secretions, but skin contamination with tattooing and vertical transmission have been reported.1,6Risk factors include close contact with a patient recently diagnosed with leprosy, immunosuppression, immunodeficiency, genetic predisposition, and exposure to armadillos.1The differential diagnosis of leprosy includes interstitial granulomatous dermatitis, granuloma annulare, granulomatous dermatitis of immune deficiency, granulomatous drug eruption, psoriasis, and other mycobacterial or fungal infections.7 The World Health Organization (WHO) classifies leprosy as multibacillary if there are 6 or more skin lesions or as paucibacillary if there fewer than 6 skin lesions.7The Ridley-Jopling classification system defines 5 categories of leprosy: tuberculoid, borderline tuberculoid, borderline, borderline lepromatous, and lepromatous.7 The clinical diagnosis of leprosy is based on the typical signs of skin lesions with hypoesthesia and nerve enlargement.7Some patients may develop an immune response toM leprae, called a leprosy reaction, which presents as urticarial swelling of skin lesions, fever, neuritis, erythema nodosum, and permanent loss of motor and sensory nerve function.2,8Leprosy reactions can occur before, during, or after treatment for leprosy.5,8 Skin biopsy is the only laboratory test that can definitively diagnose leprosy.7If skin biopsy is nondiagnostic, PCR testing of a skin biopsy specimen may be helpful. PCR has a sensitivity of 34% to 80% for paucibacillary leprosy and greater than 90% sensitivity for multibacillary leprosy, with a specificity of up to 100% for both paucibacillary and multibacillary leprosy.9 Early diagnosis and treatment are important to decrease disability and adverse psychosocial effects of leprosy and to reduce the risk of transmission.2,10The WHO recommends a 6-month course of dapsone, rifampin, and clofazimine for paucibacillary leprosy and a 12-month course for multibacillary leprosy.2Treatment with rifampin, moxifloxacin, and minocycline taken monthly for 12 to 24 months has similar efficacy, fewer adverse effects, and improved adherence compared with the WHO regimen but is 4 times more expensive.5 Leprosy relapse rates after completion of WHO multidrug therapy are 0.77% for multibacillary leprosy and 1.07% for paucibacillary leprosy.8Relapse rates appear similar after completing the regimen of rifampin, moxifloxacin, and minocycline.5Risk factors for relapse include high mycobacterial load, increased number of skin lesions, insufficient treatment duration or regimen, and poor treatment adherence.4,8 A skin biopsy sample from the patient’s arm sent to the US National Hansen’s Disease Program tested positive forM lepraeusing a quantitative PCR assay. The patient received prednisone (60 mg daily) for 5 days, then prednisone (5 mg daily) and methotrexate (20 mg weekly) to treat a leprosy reaction, which manifested as worsening paresthesia and erythema in existing skin plaques. Six days later, he started a monthly regimen of rifampin (600 mg), moxifloxacin (400 mg), and minocycline (100 mg) and received amitriptyline (10 mg) for neuropathic pain. Two months after initiation of antibiotics, the skin lesions and neuropathy symptoms had substantially improved. Eleven months after presentation, the patient underwent tendon transfer surgery with a fascia lata graft to the second through fifth fingers on his left hand, after which he completed 3 months of occupational therapy. At his most recent clinic visit, he had taken 9 of 12 planned months of rifampin, moxifloxacin, and minocycline and was taking prednisone (5 mg daily) and methotrexate (20 mg weekly).

1. Mental Demand
   Definition:

   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.

case_info.explanation: C. Send skin biopsy specimen to the US National Hansen’s Disease Program for PCR testing The key to the correct diagnosis was the presence of skin lesions with associated hypoesthesia and peripheral nerve abnormalities in a patient from Samoa, where leprosy is endemic. Choice A is incorrect because the mycobacteria causing leprosy cannot be cultured on chocolate agar.1Serologic testing forM lepraephenolic glycolipid 1 (choice B) is not commonly performed due to low sensitivity.2Choice D is incorrect because the diagnosis of leprosy must be confirmed before starting dapsone, rifampin, and clofazimine. Leprosy, also known as Hansen disease, is an infection caused by the acid-fast bacilliM lepraeandMycobacterium lepromatosis,which are obligate intracellular organisms that cannot be cultured on artificial media.1Humans are the primary carriers of infection, and in the US, the 9-banded armadillo is a zoonotic reservoir.1,3Approximately 200 000 individuals worldwide and 200 to 300 people in the US are diagnosed with leprosy annually.4,5The most common route of transmission is through respiratory secretions, but skin contamination with tattooing and vertical transmission have been reported.1,6Risk factors include close contact with a patient recently diagnosed with leprosy, immunosuppression, immunodeficiency, genetic predisposition, and exposure to armadillos.1The differential diagnosis of leprosy includes interstitial granulomatous dermatitis, granuloma annulare, granulomatous dermatitis of immune deficiency, granulomatous drug eruption, psoriasis, and other mycobacterial or fungal infections.7 The World Health Organization (WHO) classifies leprosy as multibacillary if there are 6 or more skin lesions or as paucibacillary if there fewer than 6 skin lesions.7The Ridley-Jopling classification system defines 5 categories of leprosy: tuberculoid, borderline tuberculoid, borderline, borderline lepromatous, and lepromatous.7 The clinical diagnosis of leprosy is based on the typical signs of skin lesions with hypoesthesia and nerve enlargement.7Some patients may develop an immune response toM leprae, called a leprosy reaction, which presents as urticarial swelling of skin lesions, fever, neuritis, erythema nodosum, and permanent loss of motor and sensory nerve function.2,8Leprosy reactions can occur before, during, or after treatment for leprosy.5,8 Skin biopsy is the only laboratory test that can definitively diagnose leprosy.7If skin biopsy is nondiagnostic, PCR testing of a skin biopsy specimen may be helpful. PCR has a sensitivity of 34% to 80% for paucibacillary leprosy and greater than 90% sensitivity for multibacillary leprosy, with a specificity of up to 100% for both paucibacillary and multibacillary leprosy.9 Early diagnosis and treatment are important to decrease disability and adverse psychosocial effects of leprosy and to reduce the risk of transmission.2,10The WHO recommends a 6-month course of dapsone, rifampin, and clofazimine for paucibacillary leprosy and a 12-month course for multibacillary leprosy.2Treatment with rifampin, moxifloxacin, and minocycline taken monthly for 12 to 24 months has similar efficacy, fewer adverse effects, and improved adherence compared with the WHO regimen but is 4 times more expensive.5 Leprosy relapse rates after completion of WHO multidrug therapy are 0.77% for multibacillary leprosy and 1.07% for paucibacillary leprosy.8Relapse rates appear similar after completing the regimen of rifampin, moxifloxacin, and minocycline.5Risk factors for relapse include high mycobacterial load, increased number of skin lesions, insufficient treatment duration or regimen, and poor treatment adherence.4,8 A skin biopsy sample from the patient’s arm sent to the US National Hansen’s Disease Program tested positive forM lepraeusing a quantitative PCR assay. The patient received prednisone (60 mg daily) for 5 days, then prednisone (5 mg daily) and methotrexate (20 mg weekly) to treat a leprosy reaction, which manifested as worsening paresthesia and erythema in existing skin plaques. Six days later, he started a monthly regimen of rifampin (600 mg), moxifloxacin (400 mg), and minocycline (100 mg) and received amitriptyline (10 mg) for neuropathic pain. Two months after initiation of antibiotics, the skin lesions and neuropathy symptoms had substantially improved. Eleven months after presentation, the patient underwent tendon transfer surgery with a fascia lata graft to the second through fifth fingers on his left hand, after which he completed 3 months of occupational therapy. At his most recent clinic visit, he had taken 9 of 12 planned months of rifampin, moxifloxacin, and minocycline and was taking prednisone (5 mg daily) and methotrexate (20 mg weekly).

Examination of punch biopsy samples from 2 plaques on his back revealed granulomatous periadnexal and perivascular dermatitis with diffuse granulomatous infiltrate and foamy histiocytes.
